content: 1. Everitt LS conducted a study on the introduction of a woman-held record in a hospital antenatal clinic, referred to as the Bring Your Own Records study, which was published in the Australian and New Zealand Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology. 2. Lakhani AD, Avery A, Gordon A, and Tait N evaluated the use of a home-based health record booklet, with their findings published in the Archives of Disease in Childhood. 3. Lovell A, Zander L, James CE, Foot S, Swan AV, and Reynolds A conducted a randomized controlled trial at St. Thomas’ Hospital to assess the effects of giving expectant mothers their own maternity case notes. This study was published in Paediatric and Perinatal Epidemiology in 1987. 4. Moore J, Brindle A, Goraya P, Monk S, Rennie D, Tamhne R, and colleagues developed a personal child health record for children with disabilities, with their findings published in Ambulatory Child Health in 2000. 5. Mori R, Yonemoto N, Noma H, Ochirbat T, Barber E, Soyolgerel G, and colleagues conducted a cluster-randomized controlled trial in Mongolia to evaluate the maternal and child health (MCH) handbook. Their study was published in PLoS One in 2015. 6. Osaki K, Hattori T, Toda A, Mulati E, Hermawan L, Pritasari K, and colleagues conducted a cluster-randomized study in rural Java, Indonesia, to assess the use of the MCH handbook for maternal and child care. Their findings were published in the Journal of Public Health in 2018. 7. Stille CJ, Christison-Lagay J, Bernstein BA, and Dworkin PH conducted a controlled trial to evaluate a simple provider-based educational intervention aimed at increasing infant immunization rates. This study was published in Clinical Pediatrics. 8. Usman HR, Akhtar S, Habib F, and Jehan I redesigned an immunization card and implemented center-based education to reduce childhood immunization dropouts in urban Pakistan. Their randomized controlled trial was published in Vaccine in 2009. 9. Usman HR, Rahbar MH, Kristensen S, Vermund SH, Kirby RS, Habib F, and colleagues conducted a randomized controlled trial in rural Pakistan to improve childhood immunization adherence through a redesigned immunization card and maternal education. Their findings were published in Tropical Medicine and International Health in 2011. 10. Yanagisawa S, Soyano A, Igarashi H, Ura M, and Nakamura Y conducted a community-based controlled trial in rural Cambodia to evaluate the effect of the MCH handbook on maternal knowledge and behavior. Their study was published in Health Policy and Planning in 2015. 11. Magwood O, Kpade V, Afza R, Oraka C, McWhirter J, Oliver S, and colleagues conducted a systematic review for the WHO to understand the experiences of women, caregivers, and providers with home-based records. This review was submitted for publication in 2018. 12. Byczkowski, Munafò, and Britto conducted a mixed-methods study in the USA to evaluate family perceptions of a web-based child health portal for chronic conditions like diabetes, juvenile idiopathic arthritis, and cystic fibrosis. Their findings were published in the Health Informatics Journal in 2014. 13. Clendon and Dignam conducted a descriptive retrospective study in New Zealand to assess the societal role and impact of child health and development record books, known as Plunket books, since their introduction in the 1920s. Their findings were published in the Journal of Advanced Nursing in 2010. 14. Grippo and Fracolli evaluated an educational booklet on childcare promotion in Brazil, focusing on family perceptions of health and citizenship. Their study was published in the Revista da Escola de Enfermagem in 2008. 15. Hagiwara, Ueyama, Ramlawi, and Sawada assessed the effectiveness of the MCH handbook in improving health-related behavior in Palestine. Their findings were published in the Journal of Public Health Policy in 2013. 16. Hamilton and Wyver conducted a mixed-methods study in Australia to evaluate parental use and views of the Child Personal Health Record (CPHR), also known as the Blue Book. Their findings were published in the Australian Educational and Developmental Psychologist in 2012. 17. Harrison, Heese, Harker, and Mann assessed the Road-to-Health card in South Africa based on perceptions of clinic staff and mothers. Their findings were published in the South African Medical Journal. 18. Hully and Hyne conducted a qualitative study in the United Kingdom to evaluate the use of parent-held records in a pediatric oncology unit. Their findings were published in Paediatric Nursing in 1993. 19. Hunter, McCartney, Fleming, and Guy explored the views of residential care workers in the United Kingdom on promoting the health and well-being of children in their care. Their findings were published in Adoption & Fostering in 2008. 20. Kelly, Hoonakker, and Dean conducted a mixed-methods study in the USA to evaluate the use of an inpatient portal to engage families in pediatric hospital care. Their findings were published in the Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association in 2017. 21. King, Maxwell, Karmali, Hagens, Pinto, Williams, and Adamson conducted a mixed-methods study in Canada to evaluate the use, utility, and impact of an online portal for children’s rehabilitation hospitals. Their findings were published in the Journal of Medical Internet Research in 2017. 22. Kitayama, Stockwell, Vawdrey, Pena, and Catallozzi conducted a qualitative study in the USA to explore parent perspectives on the design of a personal online pediatric immunization record. Their findings were published in Clinical Pediatrics in 2014. 23. Lee, Mulvaney-Day, Berger, Bhaumik, Nguyen, and Ward conducted a qualitative study in the USA to evaluate the Patient Passport Program for hospitalized children, focusing on care-seeking and illness management. Their findings were published in 2016. 24. O’Connor and colleagues conducted a qualitative case study in the United Kingdom to evaluate the digital version of the Personal Child Health Record (eRed Book). Their findings were published in 2016. 25. Phipps conducted a qualitative study in Australia to evaluate the use of women-held antenatal care cards, focusing on patient control, decision-making, and communication with healthcare providers. Their findings were published in 2001. 26. Quinlivan, Lyons, and Peterson conducted a mixed-methods study in Australia to evaluate obstetric patients’ preferences for a personally controlled electronic health record (PCEHR) system. Their findings were published in 2014. 27. Sharp and colleagues conducted a mixed-methods study in the USA to evaluate electronic personal health records (ePHRs) for childhood cancer survivors, focusing on knowledge, interest, and attitudes. Their findings were published in 2014. 28. Yanagisawa and colleagues conducted a mixed-methods study in Cambodia to evaluate the cultural appropriateness and potential obstacles of implementing the MCH handbook. Their findings were published in 2015.
